overview: Monte Carlo prices by brute democratic honesty: simulate the risk-neutral world many times, pay the option off in each, average, discount. For a European payoff the terminal distribution is known exactly, so this laboratory simulates one exact step — leaving sampling noise as the only error, which the model then quantifies and reports as a standard error rather than hiding. That honesty about uncertainty is the method's character: the price arrives wearing a confidence interval.

variables.name: Standard normal draws
variables.why_it_matters: The randomness. Everything else is deterministic bookkeeping; the quality of the estimate is the quality and quantity of these draws.

variables.name: Number of simulations
variables.why_it_matters: Error shrinks like 1/√n — the method's defining curse. Ten times the accuracy costs a hundred times the work, which is why variance reduction is a craft of its own.

variables.name: Antithetic partner
variables.why_it_matters: Every draw is paired with its mirror image. High and low scenarios offset, cutting variance substantially at zero extra randomness — variance reduction you can watch working in the trace.

variables.name: Standard error
variables.why_it_matters: The estimate's own honesty metric: the price is a random variable, and SE is its stated precision. Any MC result quoted without one is incomplete.

assumptions: Risk-neutral GBM dynamics — the same lognormal world as Black–Scholes.
Draws are independent and the payoff has finite variance (true for vanilla payoffs).
The fixed seed trades statistical purity for reproducibility — appropriate in a laboratory, configurable in production.
limitations: Slow convergence: 1/√n means real precision is expensive; a closed form beats it by orders of magnitude when one exists.
Greeks are hard: naive finite differences on noisy estimates are noisier still (pathwise and likelihood-ratio methods exist, at complexity cost).
For American exercise, plain MC fails outright — the continuation value needs regression techniques (Longstaff–Schwartz).
when_to_use: Path-dependent payoffs (Asians, barriers, lookbacks), multi-asset baskets, and any model too rich for closed forms — stochastic volatility, jumps, hybrid products. Dimensions are nearly free: a 30-asset basket costs barely more per path than one asset.
when_not_to_use: Vanilla European options in production (use the closed form) and early-exercise products without regression machinery.
industry_usage: The workhorse of exotics desks and XVA; effectively the only game in town once payoffs depend on paths or many underlyings.
computational_complexity: O(n) in draws; this laboratory runs 200,000 antithetic draws in a few milliseconds and reports the resulting standard error.
comparison_note: Monte Carlo differs from the closed form by sampling noise, and it tells you how much: the reported standard error. A gap inside roughly two standard errors is the method working correctly, not an error. If you need the gap smaller, quadruple the draws to halve it — the eternal 1/sqrt(n) bargain.
